entries.title: Mark 1:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: THe History of our Saviours life and death, Saint Mark is recorded to have written at the request of the Romans: In the Latin tongue say (Euseb. Hist. Eccles. l. 2. c. 15 ex Clemente. Widman stad. Epist [ilegible] dic. [ilegible]. Test. [ilegible].) some (who pretend to have seen the Originall Copie at Venice) but its more likely in Greek, a tongue (then) very well known to the Romans also. He begins with Johns Ministry, passing over Christs birth and private life for brevity sake (as it may seem) though Papists feign many idle relations thereof, and so expose us to the jears of Jewish and Turkish miscreants. There are that make Mark an Epitomator of Matthew. But forasmuch as he neither begings like Matthew, nor keeps the same order, but relateth some things that [ilegible] hath not, and other things much larger then Matthew hath them; judicious Calvin thinks (Calvin. [ilegible].) that he had not seen Saint Matthews Gospel, when he wrote his (as neither had Saint Luke seen either of them:) but that, being acted by the same spirit, they agree so harmoniously and happily; an undoubted argument of the Divinity of the Scripture, which therefore a Greek Father [ilegible] [ilegible], every way sutable (Nazianz.) to its self.

entries.title: Mark 1:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Esay and Malachi: so that there was no cause why that dead Dog Porphyry should here bark and blaspheme, as if this testimony should be falsely fathered on all the Prophets, when Esay only was the Author of it.

Behold I send my Messenger before thy face] Malachi saith, Before my face, in the person of Christ: to show that He and the Father are One.

entries.title: Mark 1:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Here Mark begins the Gospel, at the preaching of the Baptist, which the Authour to the Hebrewes begins at the preaching of Christ. Heb. 2. 3. But that is onely to prove that so great was our Saviours glory in his Miracles that it matcheth, yea surpasseth that of the Angels, those Ministers of the Law.

entries.title: Mark 1:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Like as at the promulgation of the Law, the people were commanded to wash their garments, and sanctifie themselves: so at the first publication of the Gospel, to wash their hands, and cleanse their hearts; and, in testimony of profession thereof, to beleeve and be baptised for remission of sins.

entries.title: Mark 1:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That is, a great sort of them: but John quickly grew stale to them, John 5. 35. Principium fervet, medium tepet, exitus alget. Weak-Christians easily fall off.

entries.title: Mark 1:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Elias also was a rough hairy man. Those Worthies, of whom the world was not worthy, wandered about in Sheeps skins and Goats skins, Heb. 11. but they were like the Ark, Goats hair without, but pure Gold within: or like Brutus his staffe, Cujus intus [ilegible] aurum corneo ([ilegible].) [ilegible]. [ilegible] [ilegible] cared for a better out-side, ([ilegible] comp. [ilegible].) then a rugge-gown girt close about him, yet his inside was most rich.

He did eat Locnsts] Good meat (to those there at least) though course, and easily come by. Tartarians eat the carrion-carcasles of Horses, Camels, Asses, Cats, Dogs, yea when they stink, and (Peach. Vally.) are full of Magots; and hold them as dainty, as we do Venison.

entries.title: Mark 1:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: So Jacob cryed out of old: So the Centurion, Matth. 8. So the Prodigall, Luke 15. So Peter, Luke 5. 8. So Augustin, Domine, [ilegible] dignus quem tu diligas. I am not worthy of thy love, Lord.

entries.title: Mark 1:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: When the people flocked so fast to John; that they might not mistake him for the Messias, and that his Baptisme might be the more famous.

entries.title: Mark 1:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The visible Heavens: so that the Baptist saw something above the Stars: So did Stephen; so could Christ when he was upon the earth. It is a just wonder that we can look up to so admirable an height of the starry-sky, (Burton of Melancholy.) and that the eye is not tyred in the way: Some say it is five hundred years journey to it. Other Mathematicians tell us, that if a stone should fall from the eighth Sphere, and should passe every day an hundred miles, it would be 65 years or more, before it would come to ground. ([ilegible].)

entries.title: Mark 1:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And in him with us, (Gratificavit. vu'gat.) whom he hath made gracious or Favourites in him the beloved One, Ephes. 1. 5.

entries.title: Mark 1:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That is, suddenly carrieth him (who was most [ilegible] to go) as that legall scape-Goat, Num. 16. into the Wildernesse; and there permitted him to be tempted, but supported him under the temptation, that he came safe off again. Sancti [ilegible] nequaquam [ilegible], sed toti [ilegible] imperio. The Saints are as gods. Beck & Check.

entries.title: Mark 1:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Unhurt by them: as Adam was in the state of integrity. These fell creatures saw in Christ the perfectimage of God; and therefore [ilegible] him as their Lord, as they did Adam before his fall, See Job 5. 21, 22.

entries.title: Mark 1:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: To decline Herods rage. And whereas it may seem [ilegible] Saviour herein [ilegible] a wrong course, [ilegible] Herod was Governour of [ilegible]; we must know, that the Pharisees were the men that delivered up John to Herod, Mat. 17. 11, 12. And that, but for them, there was no great [ilegible] of Herod.

entries.title: Mark 1:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: These were (Calvin. in Isaiam.) foure of our Saviours Sermon-heads. The Prophets of old were wont to set down some short notes of their larger discourses to the people, and [ilegible] them to the doores of [ilegible] Temple, till the people had read them. And then they were taken down by the Preists, and laid up for the use of posterity.

entries.title: Mark 1:16-20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Notes on Matth. 4. 18. &c.

entries.title: Mark 1:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This is noted as remarkable in Saint Mark, that he often inculcateth that our Saviour taught.

entries.title: Mark 1:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
If it could be said of Dr. (D. Hall's Epist. [ilegible]: cad. 1. Ep. 7.) Whitaker, that no man ever saw him without reverence, or heard him without wonder; How much more of Christ, sith grace was poured into his lips? Psal. 45. 2.

As one that had authority] Seest thou a Preacher deliver the Word with singular authority (as Paul, we beleeve therefore we speak) esteem him very highly for the works sake. The Corinthians are checkt, for that they were unruly, and would raign without Paul, 1 Cor. 4.

And not as the Scribes] Frigidly and jejunly. Didst thou beleeve thy self, thou wouldst never plead thy clients cause so coldly and carelesly, said Cicero to his adversary.

entries.title: Mark 1:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gr. In an unclean spirit. An unregenerate ([ilegible].) man is in maligno positus, as St. John saith of the world. He is inversus decalogus: whole evill is in man, and whole man in (1 John 5. 19.) evill, till at last (without grace) he be satanized and transformed into a breathing Devill. By reason of the inhabitation of unclean spirits, our spirits have in them Trenches Cages, Forts and strongholds of Satan, 2 Cor. 10. 4.

entries.title: Mark 1:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Not to do with Christ, and yet vex a servant of Christ? Could the Devill so mistake him, whom he confessed? It is an idle misprision, to sever the sense of an injury done to any of the members, from the head.

Thou Jesus of Nazareth] Though the Devils confessed Christ to be the Holy one of God, yet they call him Jesus of Nazareth; to nourish the errour of the multitude that thought he was born there, and so, not the Messias. Neither did the Devils cunnning fail him herein, as appears, John 7. 44.

Art thou come to destroy us?] Before the time: such is the infinite goodnesse of God, that he respits even wicked men and spirits, the utmost of their torments.

I know thee who thou art] This he spake, not to honour Christ, but to deingrate him, as commended by so lying a spirit. Laudari ab illaudato, non est laus, saith Seneca.

The holy one of God] Some rest in praysing the Sermon, and speaking fair to the Preacher. The Devill here did as much to Christ, to be rid of him. So did Herod. Mark. 6. 20.

entries.title: Mark 1:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Capistrator, be thou haltered up, or ([ilegible].) muzzled. Christ would not hear good words from an evill mouth. High words become not a fool, saith Salomon. The Lepers lips should be covered according to the Law.

entries.title: Mark 1:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
So he will serve all that he is now at inne with, as Braford hath it. You are the (Serm. of Rep. p. 70.) Devils birds (saith he to all wicked ones) whom when he hath well fed, he will broach you, and eat you, chaw you and champ you, world without end, in eternall woe and misery.

And cried with a loud voyce] But said nothing: according to verse 25.

He came out of him] With as ill a will goes the worldlings soul (Job 27. 8.) out of his body. God tears it out, as Job somewhere hath it, death makes forcible entry.

entries.title: Mark 1:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As he taught, so he wrought with ([ilegible].) authority. The same word is used verse 22.

entries.title: Mark 1:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Which the Greeks denominate of ([ilegible].) the heat that is in it: the Germans of the cold. See the Note on Matth. 8. 14.

entries.title: Mark 1:32
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And the Sabbath was ended; for till then many held it not lawfull.

entries.title: Mark 1:34
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For what calling had they to preach the Gospel?

entries.title: Mark 1:35
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The fittest time for prayer, or any ferious businesse. Therefore not only David, Psalme 5. verse 3. and other Saints, but also heathens chose the morning cheifely for Sacrifice: as Nestor in Homer, the Argonauts in Apollonius. The Persian Magi sang Hymnes to their gods at break of day, and worshipped the rising Sunne. The Pinarii and Politii sacrificed every morning and evening to Hercules, upon the great Altar at Rome, &c.

entries.title: Mark 1:38
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The neighbouring ([ilegible].) Burroughs, such as were between a City and a town. Though secret prayer were sweet to our Saviour, yet he left it to preach and profit many.

entries.title: Mark 1:40
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Morbi [ilegible] officina, saith Ambrose. We are best, when we are worst, saith another. Therefore (Camden.) King Aluored prayed God to send him alwayes some [ilegible].

entries.title: Mark 1:41
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Impensae gratiae & bonitat is signum & [ilegible], saith Calvin. And so it is of his infinite goodnesse, that he will touch our menstruous [ilegible], take at our hands our polluted performances.

entries.title: Mark 1:45
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For presse of people, [ilegible] was so frequented, that he was forced to withdraw.

entries.title: Mark 2:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: THe Sun of rightcousnesse could as little lie hid, as the Sun in Heaven.

entries.title: Mark 2:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Erasmus observeth, that Origen, in his Sermons to the people, chideth them for nothing more, then for their thin assemblies to hear the Word, and for their carelesse hearing of that, which they ought to attend to ([ilegible]. in vita Orig. operib. praefix.) with utmost diligence: recte judicans, saith he, hinc osse [ilegible] profectum aut defectum.

entries.title: Mark 2:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: apprehensis quatuor [ilegible], vivo cadaveri [ilegible]. Wicked men are living ghosts, walking Sepulchers of themselves. Bring them to Christ that they may be cured.

entries.title: Mark 2:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: By their works; as the goodnesse of the promised Land was known by the grapes and fruits, brought back by the Spyes. In all our good works, Christs eye is upon our faith, without which, it's impossible to please God.

entries.title: Mark 2:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Little do [ilegible] know when they preach, what hearers sit before them. [ilegible] fel est, quod [ilegible]. Some of our hearers carry fel in aure, as its said of some creatures, they carry their gall in their ears.

entries.title: Mark 2:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Man may remit the [ilegible], God only the transgression.

entries.title: Mark 2:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That is, by his Deity, as 1 Tim. 3. 16. Heb. 9. 14. Or, by his own spirit, as 1 Pet. 3. 8. not by inspiration, as 2 Pet 1. 21.

entries.title: Mark 2:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Christus [ilegible] divino omnia [ilegible], non injustâ aliqua virtute ac tyrannicâ. Christ did [ilegible] in his Fathers right, and not perforce.

entries.title: Mark 2:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See here our Saviours letters testimoniall, whereby he approves his authority and power to be authentick. Ye are our Epistle saith the Apostle, 1 Cor. 3. 2.

entries.title: Mark 2:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: To teach us, that nothing can be better and more usefull to the Church, then wholsome teaching; which therefore our Saviour never neglected. It was grown to a Proverb at Constantinople, Better the Sun should not shine, then Chrysostome not preach.

entries.title: Mark 2:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Our calling is of free grace, Ezeck. 16. 6. Esay 65. 1. The Scribes and Pharisees are let alone, and this Publican called to the work.

And he arose and followed him] Leaving his gainfull trade, and following his own ignominy, ruine, death. Nihil hic disputat [ilegible] vivere debeat: faith fears no famine: Christ is an universall Good, an All in all.

entries.title: Mark 2:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: All at Matthewes charge; and he thought it well bestowed, to bring them to Christ. So Paul, being himself assured of salvation, could do or suffer any thing for the salvation of his poor country-men, Rom. 8. 38, 39. with Rom. 9. 1, 2.

entries.title: Mark 2:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: They durst not say it (Horat. de Arts. Poet.) to Him: Where the hedge is lowest the beast breaks over. The Devill, as the Poet — quae desperat reniteseere posse, [ilegible]. What he hopes not to effect he never attempts.

entries.title: Mark 2:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Though not for their sakes (for hee knew it was to no purpose) yet for his other hearers sakes, he makes Apology, Jer. 3. 14, 15. God oft gives a Pastour after his own heart, for a few that are to be converted.

entries.title: Mark 2:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Beza notes that onely here and Matth. 22. 16. Luke 5. 24. is mention made in the Gospel of the Pharisees Disciples; unhappy doubtlesse in such perverse Tutors, somewhat a kin to Protagoras of whom Plato writeth that he bragged of this, that whereas he had lived threescore years, he had spent forty of them in corrupting of (Plato in Menone.) youth.

entries.title: Mark 2:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Christ is [ilegible] in ore, melos in aure, jubilum in corde. There cannot be but musick in his Temple.

entries.title: Mark 2:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Novices are not to be tied to the austerity of Religion. The Pharisees are revived in the Anabaptists, qui initiatis Christo ne risum quidem mediocrem admittunt, ([ilegible]. in Mat. 9. 15.) saith Calvin. Capistranus the Minorite, sent by the Pope into Germany and other Countries Anno 1453. to preach obedience to the See of Rome, gat a great deale of credit to his corrupt doctrine, by such a Pharisaicall severity. Sed tales Doctores meretur mundus suo fastidio veritatis, saith one, they that wil not receive the ([ilegible] in Chronolog.) truth in love, are left to the efficacy of error. 16, 17.

entries.title: Mark 2:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Notes on Matthew 9. 16, 17.

entries.title: Mark 2:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Satis salse q. d. Ignorat is adhuc, quod adeo notum & tritum. Miror ego vestram vel inscitiam, vel ignaviam. Its a shame for you, that you are yet so stupid, or so stubborn.

entries.title: Mark 2:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Though meaner men [ilegible] David.

entries.title: Mark 2:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That is, for mans safety and advantage. As he would be undone without it, hee would grow wild, and forget God: so, if it stand in the way of his safety, it is not to be observed; as if an enemy then assault us, ([ilegible] Cassius.) we may fight with him. Pompey could never have taken Jerusalem, but that the superstitious Jewes refused to defend themselves on the Sabbath: which when he observed, he then, on that day most feircely assaulted them and took their City.

entries.title: Mark 2:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This Lordship taking beginning in Christ, seems to be, from him, derived to all that are in Christ. As Psal. 8. 4, 5. compared with Heb. 2. 6, 7. Whatever David speaks of man, is applied to Christ, and so is proper to the Saints, by vertue of their union with Christ.

entries.title: Mark 3:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A Fit object inciteth and should elicite our bounty. Where God sets us up an Altar, we should be ready with our Sacrifices, with such Sacrifice God is well pleased, Heb. 13. 16.

entries.title: Mark 3:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: So carnall men do still ([ilegible].) watch and pry into professors and their conversation, 1 Pet. 3. 2. curiously observing what they may catch and carp at. But it is a brave thing to thrattle envy, to stop an [ilegible] mouth, to deny them occasion to blaspheme, as Christ did; to lead convincing lives, as (Act. and Mon) Bradford and [ilegible] did, whom neither their friends could sufficiently praise, nor their foes find any thing to fasten on.

entries.title: Mark 3:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That the miracle might be notified, and God the more glorified. It is a dishonour to a parent to hang his picture in a dark corner: so here, we should show forth the vertues of him who hath called us, 1 Pet. 2. 9.

entries.title: Mark 3:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Not to do good then, as there is opportunity, is to do evill. Qui non, cùm potest, servat, occidit. Non faciendo nocens, sed patiendo fuit, it is said of the Emperour Claudius. Not robbing only, but the not releiving of the poor, was the rich mans ruine, Luke 16. passive wickednesse is taked in some of the Churches, Rev. 2. & 3.

To save life] Gr. soule, for man, and man for the body of man. ([ilegible].) So Psal. 16. Thou wilt not leave my soule in the grave, that is, my body, as Piscator senseth it.

entries.title: Mark 3:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A sweet mixture of sinlesse passions. It is difficult to kindle, and keep quick the fire of zeal ([ilegible]. simul dolens.) without all smoke of sin.

entries.title: Mark 3:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Whom yet they hated in their hearts; but they can easily comport and comply to do Christ a mischief; as concerning that Christ pertained to Herods [ilegible].

entries.title: Mark 3:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This Country by Josephus is ([ilegible].) called Peraea, as Ultrajectum in Germany.

entries.title: Mark 3:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gr. afflict him, presse, or pinch him, as they did: a peice of his passion, verse 10.

entries.title: Mark 3:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gr. stripes, scourgings. ([ilegible]) Whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth with lesser and lighter afflictions, and scourgeth every sonne, &c. with hard and heavie (Heb 12. 6.) judgements, as plagues, banishments, persecutions, &c. Oh the (Non vulgares morbi sed saeviores, & [ilegible], qui quasiclamitant [ilegible] & [ilegible].) bloudy wailes that God hath left on the back of his best children!

entries.title: Mark 3:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The matter is well amended since Satans first on-set upon Christ. Then it was, If thou be the Son of God. The same power, when he listeth, can change the note of the Tempter to us.

entries.title: Mark 3:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Nec volentis, nec volantis, sed Dei miserantis, as a Nobleman, after Paul, gave it for his Motto. It is not in him that willeth nor in him that runneth, though he run as fast as a bird can flie: but in God that sheweth mercy.

entries.title: Mark 3:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As his houshold servants, more happy herein then those of Salomon. Christ hath many retainers, few fast and faithfull servants that follow him in the regeneration. There are those that will wear his livery, but serve themselves.

entries.title: Mark 3:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Not now, but after that famous confession of his, Matth. 16.

entries.title: Mark 3:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Syr. Benai-regeschi, filii fragoris. Naz. saith ([ilegible].) they were so called for the bignesse of their voyce. Farellus was famous for his loud speaking: when the envious Monks rang the Bells to drown his voyce as he was preaching at Metis, ille [ilegible] ad ravim usque vocem intendit, nec vinci se à strepitu ullo passus (Melch. Adam. in vita 114.) est. But there may be a great deale of force in a low language. Basill was said to thunder in his preaching, lighten in his life. Hierom was called Fulmen Ecclesiasticum, Athanasius Magues & Adamas. A Loadstone for his sweetnesse, and an Adamant for his stoutnesse. The Apostles had fiery tongues, but yet cloven. Barnabas and Boanerges, The son of Consolation and of Thunder make a good mixture. The good Samaritan poures in wine to search the sores, and oyle to supple them. Discretion must hold zeal by the heel, as Jacob did his brother: these two must be as the two Lions that supported Salomons Throne. He that hath them, may be a Moses for his meeknesse, and a Phineas for his fervour. It was a good caution that Oecolampadius gave Farellus, Evangelizatum, ([ilegible]. Epist.) non maledictum missus, &c. laudo zelum, [ilegible] non desideretur mansuetudo, &. Thou art sent, not to raile, but to reveale holy truths in meeknesse of wisdome.

entries.title: Mark 3:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Note on Matthew 10. 3.

entries.title: Mark 3:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: But could not rest (Matth. 12. 22.) in the house: for a demoniack was brought home to him, and the multitude met to hear, and Christ gratified them, with the neglect of himself. Now to all his he saith, as Abimelech did to his souldiers, What yee have seen me do, make haste and do (Judge 9 48.) as I have done.

entries.title: Mark 3:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Some read, to lay hold on the multitude, as madde because fo eager and earnest, that they left not our Lord liberty for his necessary repose and repast. But if it be meant of Christ, his mother also may seem to have been in the common errour, Uerse 31.

entries.title: Mark 3:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A devilish blasphemy, occasioned perhaps, by the former calumny of his kinsmen. What advantages make our adversaries of our smaller differences? Every subdivision is a strong weapon in the hand of the contrary party.

entries.title: Mark 3:23-25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Note on Matth. 12. 25, 26.

entries.title: Mark 3:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: and yet Bellarmine teacheth, that the sin against the holy Ghost may be forgiven, Lib. 2. de poenitentia cap. 16. But it may be he was of their opinion (Dan. Hist. of Engl. fol. 163.) that taught here in England in the reign of Henry 3. that to question the Popes sanctions, was the sinne against the holy Ghost.

entries.title: Mark 3:31
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Here the Evangelist returneth to the History he had begun to set forth, verse 21.

entries.title: Mark 3:33
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Bishop Ridley is likewise (Acts & Mon. fol. 1559.) said to have been very kind to his kinsfolks, yet not bearing with them any otherwise then right would require.

entries.title: Mark 4:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: MInisters must like wise fetch comparisons from things most familiar, and best known to their hearers: as the Prophets from when they have to deale with the Egyptians, from flocks and herds; when with the Arabians, from Merchandise and Navigation; when with the Tyrians and Sidonians, &c. And as our Saviour from fishing, when he dealeth with fishers: from sowing when with seedsmen, &c.

entries.title: Mark 4:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Christ well knew the ficklenesse of mens spirits, and how every small matter calls them off, when most earnestly set to hear: See the Note on Matth. 13. 3.

entries.title: Mark 4:4-5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Notes on Matth. 13. 3, 4, 5, &c.

entries.title: Mark 4:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This is spoken in ([ilegible].) opposition to the thorny ground, where the thorns grow up together with the corn, and over-top it: Whereas the good ground brings forth fruit increasing, and ascending: and although it have many thorns, yet grace is superiour to corruption, and keeps it under.

entries.title: Mark 4:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That are in the Church, but not of the Church. Shee hath her hang-byes, that are as Wens or botches to the body.

entries.title: Mark 4:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Note on Matth. 13, 14, &c. ([ilegible] alias [ilegible].)

entries.title: Mark 4:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As children run away with sweet-meats. But the new-birth is seldome without pain, and without a flux of mortification. Leap-Christians prove Apostates.

entries.title: Mark 4:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Or lighted, q. d. Take the benefit of the light of the Gospel, suffer it not to stand under a bed or bushell: for there is nothing hid, viz. in our hearts but it shall be opened, viz. by the power of the word most plainly. Lex, lux, the word is a curious critick, Heb. 4. 12.

entries.title: Mark 4:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
As the husbandman is very curious in the choyce of his seed.

Verse Ibid. Shall more be given] sc. If you bring with you a [ilegible] of your former hearings. He that hears as he ought, every time he hears he grows something more rich: he picks up the Gospels pearls, and presents them to God the next time, that he may have more. The good soul cannot be without some daily comings in from Christ.

entries.title: Mark 4:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Grace grows by exercise, and impairs by idlenesse: As that side of the teeth (John 1.) which is least used in chewing, is apt to have more rhume settle upon (Rom. 1.) it. Though both armes grow, yet that which a man useth, is the stronger and bigger: so is it in grace. God giveth grace for grace, and his righteousnesse is revealed from faith to faith: that is, from a lesse measure to a greater. Whereas it is easie to observe an Eclipse and decay of Gods gifts in them that use them not, till at last they may say with Zedekiah, When went the spirit of God from me?

entries.title: Mark 4:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: God sows and reaps in the Church, though none observes it, and hath his fruit in due season.

entries.title: Mark 4:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Ministers must rest secure of the successe of their endeavours, having diligently done their duties. The Word may work many a year after: as they say of the Elephant, that she brings not forth till thirteen years after shee hath conceived.

entries.title: Mark 4:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And the husbandman looks upon it with delight, in hope of an harvest: so doth God take in good part our weak beginnings, whiles we strive to better the blessing that is upon our very buds. Esay 44. 3. The first springs in the womb of grace are precious to him, Ephes. 2. 1.

entries.title: Mark 4:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The wisdome of God, the great Counsellour, seems to be at a fault for a fit expression low enough for our slow apprehension.

entries.title: Mark 4:33
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Not as he was able to have spoken. A Minister must masticate his matter as Nurses do their childrens meat, and speak to his hearers shallow capacities; or else he shall be a Barbarian to them, and they to him. He's the best Preacher saith Luther, that preacheth vulgarly, trivially, &c.

entries.title: Mark 4:34
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: He read them the riddles, as it were, ([ilegible].) or untied the knots. So Judg. 7. 15. We read of a dream and the interpretation, or breaking of it. A metaphor from the breaking of a Nut to get the kernell.

entries.title: Mark 4:36
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Viz. out of that part of the Ship where he had taught, into another part more convenient, where he might rest. For he had preached all that day till the evening, without taking either repast or repose, verse 1.

entries.title: Mark 4:38
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Neither did the noyse of the sea, nor the hurry of the seamen labouring for life, awake Christ, till his own time was come. Despaire not, if help be not at hand at first; as we desire: but awake Christ, as here, and Esay 51. 9. God hath a mighiy arme, but, it may be asleep; the Church therefore cryes three times in a verse, Awake.

entries.title: Mark 4:39
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That is, have done quickly: so much the ingemination imports, Gen. 41. 32.

entries.title: Mark 4:40
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Increpatio cum admiratione: ([ilegible] tempestatem: [ilegible], & [ilegible]. Plut.) As their, Master, carest thou not, &c. was interrogatio conquerentis & reprehendentis. But if Caesar in a tempest could bid the Barge-man be of good chear, for he carried over the fortune of Caesar, which could not miscarry; how much more might those that were upon the same bottom with Christ, have beene confident of a safe arrivall?

entries.title: Mark 5:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: GRaecè. In an unclean spirit, quod eum spiritus quasi inclusum ([ilegible].) [ilegible]. So the flesh is called the old man, as if it were the whole (Beza.) of a naturall man: and the Devill is said to work effectually in such, Ephes. 2. 2. See the Note on Mark 1. 23.

entries.title: Mark 5:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The buriallplaces of the Saints were anciently thought to have a kind of holinesse in them. Hence grew that superstition of meeting and praying together at the Saints Sepulchers; and afterwards of praying for them, and to them. Which to foment the Devill usually haunted such places, there to play his pranks.

entries.title: Mark 5:4-6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Notes on Matth. 8. 28.

entries.title: Mark 5:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Exemplum horrendum impudentiae sceleratorum spirituum, saith Beza. To adjure one, is to take an oath of him for our own security. An oath is not rashly to be undertaken, but by a kind of necessity, when it is exacted. Hence the Hebrew Nishbang is a passive, and signifieth To be sworn, rather then to swear.

entries.title: Mark 5:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That is, a multitude. A [ilegible] was commonly among the Romans saith (Isidore) six thousand armed souldiers. So many Devils were gotten in one poor man. Let us in him see, what the best of us have deserved: and, sith we have escaped, offer a Passe over each for himself.

entries.title: Mark 5:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: All this Country was full of hills (intercursantibus montibus Galaad) and mountaines of Gilead.

entries.title: Mark 5:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
If Christ condescended to the Devils, though to the losse of others, will he not hear us?

Into the Sea] So that standing pool in Gadaris is called, which, (Strabo Geog. lib. 16.) Strabo saith, is of such a naughty nature, that if beasts taste of it they shed their hair, nails, hoofs or horns.

entries.title: Mark 5:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
And, amazed with the miracle, they expostulate not an injury; but acknowledging him Lord of all, they beg him to be gone, lest they should sustain further losse by him: The Devill shall have his dwelling again in themselves rather then in their pigges (as that martyr phrased (Bradford.) it) they will rather lose Christ then their porket.

And in his right mind] Sanguis medici factus est medicina phrenetici. The Surgions bloud was the sick mans salve.

entries.title: Mark 5:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Note on Mat. 8. 34.

entries.title: Mark 5:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This was all the fee Christ lookt for, for his cures. Words seem to be a slender and slight recompence: but Christ (saith Nazianzen) calleth himself the Word.

entries.title: Mark 5:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A great mercy to them to have such a Preacher sent amongst them. Bethsaida was denied this favour, Mark 8. 26.

entries.title: Mark 5:22-24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Notes on Matth. 9. 18. &c.

entries.title: Mark 5:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This History fell out fitly, that Jairus might be confirmed, and the different degrees of faith in severall Saints, the better discerned.

entries.title: Mark 5:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Physitians are many (Plaut.) of them crumenimulgae, & fordida poscinummia. They call their drugs [ilegible], gifts: yet we pay dear for them. Jurisconsultorum idem status & Medicorum: Damna quibus licito sunt aliena lucro. Hi morbos aegrorum, agrorum litibus illi (Owen. [ilegible].) Dant patienter opem, dum potiantur opum. Howbeit their greedy desire of money seldome prospereth with them. Dicis te medicum, nos te plus esse fatemur: (Mendico sc. Ibid.) Una tibi plus est littera quam medico.

entries.title: Mark 5:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Note on Mat. 9. 21.

entries.title: Mark 5:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As heat goeth out of the Sun into the ayre, water, earth, earthly bodies, and yet remains in the Sun; so here. Salienti aquarum fonti undas si tollas, nec exhauritur, nec extenuatur, sed dulcescit: [ilegible], etiam docendi officio, dulcedinem [ilegible], non sentiat minutias. A fountain is not drawn dry, but cleared: so skill is not lost by communicating it to others, but increased.

entries.title: Mark 5:32
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: He confuted the rashnesse of his Disciples, not with words, but looks. We may more fitly sometimes signifie our dislike of sin by frowns, then by speeches. As the North-wind drives away rain, &c.

entries.title: Mark 5:34
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: They that can shame themselves to honour Christ, shall receive much settlement, and inward satisfaction.

entries.title: Mark 5:35
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Christ commonly reserves his holy hand for a dead lift.

entries.title: Mark 5:40
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Note on Matth. 9. 24. &c.

entries.title: Mark 5:43
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Lest he should be too soon known and acknowledged by the people. But when he knew that he was shortly to die, he openly restored to life Lazarus, and the Widows son. Every thing is beautifull in its season. (Eccles. 3.)

entries.title: Mark 6:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: SEe the Note on Matthew 13. 55.

entries.title: Mark 6:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: He could not, because he would not. Note here the venernous nature of infidelity, that transfuseth, as it were, a dead palsie into the hands of omnipotency, disabling Christ, in a sort, to do such a man good. Christ by his absolute power can do all things: by his actuall power he can do no more then he will do.

entries.title: Mark 6:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Unbeleife must needs be a monstrous sin, that puts Christ to the marvell.

entries.title: Mark 6:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Such a one as may ease and releive you, not such as may curb and hinder you, Matth. 10. 10. So that seeming contradiction is assoyled.

No money in your purses] Gr. No brasse in your girdles. The ([ilegible].) most usuall materiall of money among the Roman Princes was seldome gold or silver, most times brasse, sometimes leather, Corium [ilegible] publicâ [ilegible], as Seneca hath it. The like is said to have been used here in England, in the times of the Barons Wars. And why not? sith Opinion sets the price upon these outward good things; and Anno 1574. the Hollanders, then being in their (Hist. of [ilegible].) extremities, made mony of past-board.

entries.title: Mark 6:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This must be done; or men are utterly undone. Aut poenitendum aut pereudum. Hence Repentance is so pressed and preached in both Testaments. Exod. 23. 20. with 33. 2. 3, 4. Immediately after God had given the Law (by the rules and threats whereof God the Father was to proceed, saith One) and after they had transgressed it, he could not go along with them, for he should destroy them: but his Angel, that is Christ, he would send with them; who also would destroy them, if they turned not and repented according to the rules of his Law, the Gospel.

entries.title: Mark 6:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: By the misunderstanding of this text, and that Jam. 5. 14. Pro pastoribus habuit ([ilegible] Confess.) Ecclesia unguentarios, et pigmentarios; qui hoc [ilegible] miser as oviculas non tantum ungerent, sed etiam emungerent. This oyl in the text was used, not as a medicine, but as a sign and symbol of that power of miraculous [ilegible].

entries.title: Mark 6:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: By miracles, as by wings the Gospel quickly spred far and neer. Eusebius saith that the ([ilegible].) Gospel spred at first, through the world, like a Sun [ilegible]. When (Euseb l. 2. c. 3.) [ilegible] first stirred, it was carried through the Christian world, as on Angels wings. This was that miracle, which [ilegible] these last times, are to look for.

entries.title: Mark 6:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Notes on Matt. 14. 2, 3, &c.

entries.title: Mark 6:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gr. Hung over ([ilegible].) him, as highly displeased at him, and waiting an occasion to be even with him. [ilegible], they that follow truth close at heeles, may have their [ilegible] struck out, though she be a good mistrisse. Tange [ilegible]. As wild beasts cannot endure fire, so neither can carnall hearts fervency and plaindealing.

entries.title: Mark 6:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Holinesse is majesticall. [ilegible] because holy. He honoureth his Saints in the [ilegible] of their greatest enemies.

He did many [ilegible]] [ilegible], [ilegible] some copies have it, He doubted in many things: he was often set at a stand, and knew not how ([ilegible] multum [ilegible].) to ward off the dry-blows of the word, [ilegible] which way to look, it came so close to him.

entries.title: Mark 6:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The ancients took a light dinner usually, and therefore called it Prandium quasi perendium: at supper they feasted more freely, and therefore called it [ilegible], because then their daies-work was done.

entries.title: Mark 6:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: With immodest gesticulations ([ilegible] [ilegible], [ilegible] more.) and trippings on the toe, wherewith the old fornicator was so inflamed, that he swore she should have any thing of him.

entries.title: Mark 6:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: What was his whole kingdom to the life of that precious man, of whom the world was not worthy? Shortly after, he was turned out of his kingdom, and (its to be feared) out of Gods too.

entries.title: Mark 6:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The men and women dined not together. In Barbary, tis death for any man to see one of the Zeriffes concubines.

entries.title: Mark 6:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Sic plerique, malum iter ingressi, post cum se errare resciscant, non desciscunt [ilegible], ne leves videantur: sui dicti domini, ut dicunt, esse volunt. ([ilegible].) Some, rather then be worse then their words, will violate their consciences.

entries.title: Mark 6:31
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: God would not have the strength of his people to be exhausted in his service: but that respect be had to the health of their bodies, as to the welfare of their [ilegible]. Therefore the Priests of the Law took their turns of serving in the order of their course, as Zacharias, [ilegible] 1. 8. And the Ministers of the Gospel are allowed to drink a little Wine for their healths sake as Timothy. Those that neglect their bodies, must reckon for it. Coloss. 2. 23.

entries.title: Mark 6:33
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That is, they came thither by land, not by sea; whither on foot or a [ilegible]: for many of ([ilegible] ubique opponuntur. Scultet.) them were not able to foot it, as being weak, lame, maymed, &c.

entries.title: Mark 6:34
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: They were all slaves to the Romans, and many of them lame and diseased: but nothing troubled Christ so much as this, that they wanted Pastours and Teachers. They that are without a teaching Preist, are said to be without God in the world, 2 Chron. 15. 3.

entries.title: Mark 6:35
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Beza renders it, Cum jam multus dies esset. Our forefathers had a saying The Summers day is never so long, But at length' twill ring to even-song.

entries.title: Mark 6:37
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: q. d. Yes: a likely [ilegible] surely: Where's your mony? have we two-hundred pence to cater for such a company? It is Interrogatio cum admiratione, atque adeo cum ironia quadam conjuncta, saith Beza. A question not without a jear.

entries.title: Mark 6:40
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gr. rankes, rankes; that is, ([ilegible]. Hebraismus, ut Exod. [ilegible]. 14.) [ilegible] by rank, as rowes or borders of beds in a garden. Ordinatim [ilegible] in Ecclesia faciendae. Church-work is to be done decently, and in order.

entries.title: Mark 6:48
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Either the more to try them, or rather to spare them: because he foresaw they would be further frighted else.

entries.title: Mark 6:50
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: I with an Emphasis: q. d. It is I; not a (Cant. 2. [ilegible].) Spirit. A concise kind of speech, importing his haste to comfort them. He comes leaping over the mountaines of Bether, all [ilegible] and impedements.

entries.title: Mark 7:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: THey mumped at it, as we say: they dispraised, accused, complained. ([ilegible].) Vituperant homines quam collaudant promptius, saith one: Another being demanded, what was the easiest thing in the world? answered, To find fault with another. [ilegible], saith a Third: It is easier to find a fault, then to mend it.

entries.title: Mark 7:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Or up to the Elbow, or with utmost diligence. The Pharisees deemed it as great ([ilegible] & accurate. Syr.) a [ilegible] to eate with unwashen [ilegible], as to commit fornication. Do not our Modern Pharisees the Papists as much? Fornication (Godwins Antiq. Heb. p. 49.) is a mony matter with them: but to eate an Egge in Lent, or the like, a deadly sin. You may see them sometimes in Italy go along the streets with a great rope about their necks, as if they were dropped down from the gallowes. And sometimes they wear a sawsedge or a swines-pudding in place of a silver or gold chain. (Bee-hive of Rome. p. 24.) Is not this sufficient to deserve heaven by?

entries.title: Mark 7:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gr. Baptismes. The Pharisees ([ilegible].) were great washers of the out-side. Whence Justin Martyr calls ([ilegible].) them Baptists, by a peculiar Epithite.

entries.title: Mark 7:5-6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Note on Matt. 15. 2, 3.

entries.title: Mark 7:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gr. With tooth and ([ilegible].) naile ye hold it, Mordicus retinetis, as if on that hinge hung all your happinesse.

entries.title: Mark 7:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: q. d. Its finely done of you, is ([ilegible] Sane benè.) it not? Ironicè; yeare wise men therewhile: This was [ilegible] to other masterships. Sapientes sapienter in infernum [ilegible], saith a Father. The worlds wizards have not wit enough to escape hell.

entries.title: Mark 7:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: i. e. Ye license him to deny his Parents any further succour.

entries.title: Mark 7:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For he saw there was no good to be done upon the Pharisees, and that he did but wash a tilestone, or a Blackmoore: he turns him therefore to the commonsort. Pearls must not be cast to pigs.

entries.title: Mark 7:15-16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Note on Matt. 15. 11.

entries.title: Mark 7:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Or into the long ([ilegible].) and lowermost gut, as Physitians use the word: and as it is, 1 Sam. 5. 9. 12. Robert Smith Martyr made one of Bonners Doctors that examined him, say, that his God must needs enter into the belly, and so fall into the draught. To which he Answered, What derogation was it to Christ, when the Jewes spit in his face? If the Jewes (said Smith) being his enemies did but spit in his face, [ilegible], we being his friends throw him into the draught, which of us deserveth (Act. & Mon. fol. 1536.) the greater damnation?

entries.title: Mark 7:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Farre worse then any jakes. Sinne is the Devils excrement.

entries.title: Mark 7:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Envious, and rejoycing at the miseries ([ilegible] [ilegible], [ilegible]. q. [ilegible].) of others, which is the property of Edomites, abjects, witches, and devills. Those that are bewitched are said to be over-lookt, sc. with an evill and malicious eye. [ilegible] quis teneros, &c.

entries.title: Mark 7:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Should God but break open that sink of sin that is within us, we should never indure the stench, but rid our selves out of the world, as Judas, Ahitophel, &c.

entries.title: Mark 7:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
There was therefore two wills in Christ: the one whereof rightly willed, that which the other justly and wisely nilled.

But he could not be hid] He is a God that [ilegible] himself: we ([ilegible] 8. 17.) must fetch him out of his retiring roome by our [ilegible] prayers.

entries.title: Mark 7:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Of an heroicall faith, felt her want of Christ, and [ilegible] out for him.

entries.title: Mark 7:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gr. unto whelps, for more ([ilegible].) contempt-sake, as Beza [ilegible]. The Pope made Dondalus the ([ilegible]. p. 379.) [ilegible] Embassadour to come before him, tied in iron chains, and to wallow under his table with dogs, whilest his Holinesse sate at supper. Unde ei Canis cognomentum apud suos, saith Kevius. He (De viis pontif.) was ever after called the Dog-Embassadour.

entries.title: Mark 7:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Note on Matth. 15. 27.

entries.title: Mark 7:33
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Though these mens faith was but weak, yet he yeeldeth unto them at the first word, who held off the Syrophenisse before, to the third Petition: Hee knew the strength of her faith. The skilfull Armourer trieth not an ordinary peece of Armes with Musquet shot. The wise Lapidist brings not his softer stones to the stithy. The good Husbandman turnes not the wheele upon his cumin, nor his [ilegible] upon his fetches. For his God doth better instruct him, Esay 28. 26, 29.

entries.title: Mark 7:34
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As if himself had felt and fainted under ([ilegible].) the same burden: so the word signifieth. And he was so much the more sensible, as well weighing the cause.

entries.title: Mark 7:35
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: So are the eares of all that belong to Christ, and their tongues loosed to his praise, which before were bound by Satan. O pray that God would make the boare of our eares as wide as may be, and teach us that pure language, Zeph. 3. 9. that our tongues may run as the pen of a ready (Psal. 45. 1.) writer.

entries.title: Mark 7:36
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Eò magis praefulgebat utique quia non visebatur, as Tacitus saith of Brutus: the more he sought to secret himself, the more he was noticed.

entries.title: Mark 7:37
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Praise we him much more for his spirituall cures, of like kind, upon our selves and others.

entries.title: Mark 8:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: YEt not so great as the five thousand before fed with fewer loaves, and more leavings: To teach us, that Gods blessing, and not the muchnesse of meat, feeds and satisfies.

entries.title: Mark 8:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Notes on Matthew 15. 32, 33, 34, &c.

entries.title: Mark 8:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Their sine [ilegible] will be loosened, as it useth ([ilegible].) to fare with men in fainting fits. Physitians sometimes let bloud usque ad deliquium animae: so doth God; as he did David often. See the Note on Matth 15. 32.

entries.title: Mark 8:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That is, with the coursest fare. [ilegible] opponit panem libis & placentis. Lib. 1. Ep. 10. Bread is used for homely provision.

entries.title: Mark 8:5-7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Notes on Matth. 15. 34, 35, 36.

entries.title: Mark 8:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
His heart was straightned (as ([ilegible]) the word signifies) and would have burst, but for a vent. Expletur lachrymis egeriturque dolor. (Ezek. 9. 4.)

So those marked mourners sighed and cried for others, who were altogether insensible of their own miseries. So Habacuc trembled and quivered for the Chaldeans calamities, cap. 3. 16.

entries.title: Mark 8:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Notes on Matthew 16. 1, 2.

entries.title: Mark 8:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Of the Sadduces saith Matthew: to the which Sect some conceive that Herod had now joyned himself, the better to still the noise of his conscience, by making himself beleeve there was no judgement to come.

entries.title: Mark 8:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: All's loft that is not well laid up in this pot of Mannah, the sanctified memory, 1 Cor. 15. 2.

entries.title: Mark 8:19-20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Note on Matth. 16. 10, 11, &c.

entries.title: Mark 8:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: It is very ill taken when we improve not experiments. Of all things God can least abide to be forgotten.

entries.title: Mark 8:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
He could have delivered him to his friends, to lead him; but he did it himself, as holding it an honour, a pleasure, to do men in misery any office of curtesie.

And led him out of the town] Either that the miracle he wrought might be the lesse noticed: or as holding the inhabitants unworthy to behold it. All Israel might see [ilegible] go towards the Rock of Rephidim, none but the Elders might see him strike it. Their unbeleif made them unworthy this priviledge: so might their unthankfulnesse the men of Bethsaida. Wo to thee [ilegible]. It is no small favour of God to make us witnesses of his great works.

entries.title: Mark 8:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Procul & dilucidè, longè ([ilegible]) [ilegible]. When we come to heaven we shall see as we are seen, who now see but as in a glasse obscurely, as old men do thorough Spectacles, 1 Cor. 13.

entries.title: Mark 8:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Christ would not vouchsafe such an ungratefull people the benefit of one more Preacher, though never so mean. This was a greater judgement upon them, then if he had turned some other way that arme of the sea that brought so much wealth into their town.

entries.title: Mark 8:27-28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See the Note on Matth. 16. 13.

entries.title: Mark 8:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This was much in few. Here is not Thou art Peter, and upon this Rock, &c. Which if either Saint Mark or Saint Peter had esteemed (as Papists now do) the foundation of the Christian Church, it had not been here omitted (as Beza well observeth) sith it goes for currant among the Ancients, that Saint Mark wrote this Gospel at Saint Peters mouth.

entries.title: Mark 8:31
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That is, within three dayes, or on the third day.

entries.title: Mark 8:34
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
See the Notes on Mat. 10. 38. and Mat. 16. 24.

Take up his Crosse] It is but a delicacy that men dream of to (Joh. de Polemar. [ilegible]. in Concil. [ilegible]. ap. Binnium.) divide Christ and his Crosse. Every Christian must be a Crucian, said Luther; and do somewhat more then those Monks that made themselves woodden Crosses, and carried them on their backs continually, making all the world laugh at them.

entries.title: Mark 8:35
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As that revolting [ilegible], Host to Philbert [ilegible] Martyr, slaine by his enemy upon a private quarrell. As those Angrognians that yeelded to the Papists (Act. & Mon. fol. 835.) that came against them, and were more cruelly handled by them then their neighbours that continued constant in the truth. As Denton the Smith of Welle in Cambridgshire, that could not burn (Ibid. 873.) for Christ, and was afterwards burned in his own house. As West (Ibid. 1558.) that was Chaplaine to Bishop Ridly, who refusing to dye in Christs cause with his Master, said Masse against his conscience, and soone (Ibid. 1570.) after pined away for sorrow. If I shrink from Gods truth (said Doctor Taylor Martyr) I am sure of another manner of death then had Judge Hales: who being drawn for fear of death, to do (Ibid. 1382.) things against his conscience, did afterwards drowne himselfe.

entries.title: Mark 8:36
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And yet many do as Shimei that to seek his servants, lost himself. And as Jonas, that was content to be cast into the Sea, that the Ship with her lading might come safe to shore.

entries.title: Mark 8:38
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
The worse the times are, the better we should be. Stars are most needed in a dark night. We may as well, saith Zuinglius, Adaram Jovis aut Veneris adorare, ac sub Antichristo fidem occultare. Antichrists limbs have their mark in their hand, which they may shew or hide at pleasure: but Christs members have their mark in their foreheads only. Davids parents and brethren came down to him, to the cave of Adullam though to their great danger, 1 Sam. 22. 1. Onesiphorus was not ashamed of Pauls chain at Rome, 2 Tit. 1.

When he commeth in the glory] David going against Goliah took only his sling, and a few stones; but when against Nabal, he marched better appointed. So Christ came at first in a mean condition: but when he comes again to judgement, he shall march furiously, attended with troops of Saints and Angels.

entries.title: Mark 9:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: SAints only taste of death, sinners are swallowed up of it, they are killed with death, Revelation 2. 23. Whereas the righteous do mori vitaliter; death is to them neither totall, nor perpetuall, Rom. 8. 10, 11. ([ilegible].)

entries.title: Mark 9:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gr. Glistring and sparkling as stars which twinckle and beckon to us as it were to remember their and our Creatour.

entries.title: Mark 9:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: With much adoe they ([ilegible].) kept it (as the word imports) for the rest of the Disciples were very inquisitive, likely, what was said and done in the Mount. A friend that can both keep counsell, and give counsell, is worth his weight in gold.

entries.title: Mark 9:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Vilified and nullified as an [ilegible], ([ilegible].) or one that had nothing in him. Vermis sum et non [ilegible]. I am a worm and no man, saith the Psalmist in the person of Christ.

entries.title: Mark 9:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: To see him come in so opportunly, in the very nick, which is his usuall time. See the Note on Matt. 17. 14.

entries.title: Mark 9:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thus things oft goe backward ere they come forward; as the corn grows downward before it comes upward. Duplicantur lateres, venit Moses. This child had never such a sore fit, as now that he was to be cured. See verse 26.

entries.title: Mark 9:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
So doth blind zeal deal by them in whom it is.

But if thou canst doe any thing] This wofull father had no further patience to parley; but through weaknesse of faith, and strength of affection to his distressed child breaks off his tale, and begs present help. Hee that beleeveth, maketh no haste, Esay 28. 16.

entries.title: Mark 9:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
This act of his in putting forth his faith to beleeve as hee could, was the way to beleeve as hee would.

Help thou mine unbeleefe] That is, my weak faith, which hee counteth no better then unbeleef: howbeit, God counts the preparation of the heart to beleeve, faith: as in those Samaritanes Joh. 4. Doctor Cruuger cryed out on his death-bed, Credo languidà (Selnever. [ilegible].) fide, sed tamen fide. Much faith will yeeld unto us here our heaven: and any faith, if true, will yeeld us heaven hereafter.

entries.title: Mark 9:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The cause why they could not cure the child, was unbeleef: the cure of unbeleef is sought and wrought by fasting and prayer.

entries.title: Mark 9:34
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: viz. In Christs earthly Kingdom, in the which they vainly dreamt of a distribution of honours and offices, as once in the dayes of David and Solomon.

entries.title: Mark 9:37
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Non removet, sed corrigit, saith Erasmus. He receiveth not me only, but him that sent me.

entries.title: Mark 9:38
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: John was soon sated with that sad discourse of our Saviour, and begins a relation of another businesse, little to the purpose.

entries.title: Mark 9:39
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: It is probable that this man would not forbear, unlesse Christ himself should forbid him: which here he refuseth to do, and shewes reason for it.

entries.title: Mark 9:41
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Much more he that shall cast out devils in my name, and out of love to me.

He shall not lose his reward] For his cup of cold water he shall have a torrent of pleasure. If therefore ye will be wise Merchants, happy Usurers, part with that which ye cannot keep, that ye may gain that which ye cannot lose.

entries.title: Mark 9:43
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
The Trojanes, after long debate, concluded it better to part with Helen, though a Lady of incomparable beauty, then, by retaining her longer, to venture their utter wreck and ruine.

'A[ilegible], say they. Did we but forethink (Hom. Iliad.) what sinne will cost us, we durst not but be innocent.

entries.title: Mark 9:44
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
As out of the corruption of our bodies wormes breed, which consume the flesh, so out of the corruption of our soules this never-dying worme. This worme (say Divines) is only a continuall remorse and furious reflection of the soule upon its own wilfull folly, and now wofull misery. Oh consider this before thy friends be scrambling for thy goods, worms for thy body, devils for thy soule. Goe not dancing to hell in thy bolts, rejoyce not in thy bondage, as many doe; to whom the preaching of hell is but as the painting of a toad, which men can look on and handle, without affrightment.

Never dyeth, and the fire is not quenched] O quam diuturna & (Manlii loc. com pag. 33.) immensa est [ilegible] as! said the devill once. A child with a spoon may sooner empty the sea, then the damned accomplish their misery. A [ilegible] of brimstone is not consumed by burning.

entries.title: Mark 9:49
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The Spirit, as salt, must dry up those bad humours in us that breed the neverdying worm; and, as fire, must waste our corruptions, which else will carry us on to the unquenchable fire.

entries.title: Mark 9:50
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Nature [ilegible] prudently mingled salt with all things, that they may not easily putrifie. Greges enim (Joh. Bodin.) pecorum urinam salsissimam effundere videmus, & in omnes stirpes ([ilegible]. [ilegible].) salem infusum.

Have salt in your selves] Habete in vobis sal. A [ilegible] admonemur tribus literis (ut curiosè observat quidam) Sapere, Agere, Loqui. The conjuring of salt among the Papists is intolerably blasphemous: It is thus: I conjure thee, O salt, by the living God, &c. that thou maist be made a conjured salt to the salvation of them that beleeve. And that unto all such as receive thee, (Act. & Mon.) thou mayest be health of soul and body: and [ilegible] from out of the place, wherein thou shalt be sprinkled, may fly away and depart all phantasie, wickednesse or craftinesse of the devils subtilty, and every foule Spirit, &c.

And [ilegible] peace one with another] By mortification season, tame, and purge your own hearts of those lusts that warre in your members, Jam. 4. 1. and prove offensive to others, Mar. 9. 43. so shall you be at peace one with another. Stomack-worms are killed with salt.

entries.title: Mark 10:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: PRaedicationis officium [ilegible] quisquis ad Sacerdotium accedit. (Greg. in [ilegible].) It was death for the High-Priest to enter the Holy-place, or to come abroad, without his bells and pomegranates. Saint Mark is much in setting forth Christs forwardnesse to teach.

entries.title: Mark 10:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Not commanded. There is difference between a permission and a precept, properly so called. See the Note on Matth. 19. 7. Non statim probat Deus quod permittit. God approves not presently whatsoever hee permits.

entries.title: Mark 10:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Annon columnae [ilegible], [ilegible] Lutherus, [ilegible] errarunt, & [ilegible] se dederunt, cum illud [ilegible] dederunt ([ilegible]. [ilegible]. epist. dedicat.) [ilegible] illi & [ilegible] Principi Philippo Lantgravio, ut [ilegible] adhue priore legitima [ilegible] uxore, [ilegible] alteram, [ilegible] est adulteram? saith Zanchy: Luthor and his fellow-Divines were shamefully out in licensing the Lantgrave to put away his lawfull wife, and marry another.

entries.title: Mark 10:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: No such thing was permitted by Moses, but usurped by the women of those licentious times. Among Turkes the women may sue a divorce; but (Blunts [ilegible].) only then when her husband would abuse her against nature.

entries.title: Mark 10:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As oft therefore as we see an infant, [ilegible] us think that a teacher is given us of God. Psal. 131. 1, 2.

entries.title: Mark 10:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Doe no man injury either by force [ilegible]. This seems to be an abstract of all the other fore-mentioned commandements.

entries.title: Mark 10:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As a [ilegible] man, and fit to live in a civill society. Or hee loved him, that is, hee pitied him, as a self-deceiver: like as we pity moderate Papists.

entries.title: Mark 10:22
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Which hee would not have done, if he had loved God and his neighbour, as he professed to doe.

entries.title: Mark 10:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As most rich men doe, thinking themselves simply the better and the safer for them. This blab is soon blown up.

entries.title: Mark 10:27
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This place is much pleaded by the Papists for their fiction of Transubstantiation. I tell thee (said Bonner to Philpot) that God by his omnipotency (Act. & Mon.) may make himself to be this Carpet, if he will.

entries.title: Mark 10:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Mothers he cannot receive in kind, when once dead; but God will be to his better then ten mothers: Communion with him shall yeeld more comfort, then all outward comforts can. He can also make Jonathan more loving to David then any wife, and the Kings of Moab and Ammon to be his foster-parents. This made Hermannus (Act. & Mon. [ilegible]. 815.) Archbishop of Cullen to reform his Church, using therein the aid and advice of Martin Bucer: Wherefore he was deposed by the Emperor, which he patiently suffered. Zech. 10. 6. They shall be as if I had not cast them off, and I will heare them. God will one way or other make up his peoples losses: they shall have it again either in money, or moneys-worth. Ne excrucier ob [ilegible] (Aug [ilegible] civit.) & argentum: [ilegible] enim es mihi omnia, said Paulinus Nolanus, (Dei. lib. 1. c. [ilegible].) when the Town was taken by the Barbarians. Let not my losses trouble me, Lord; for thou art mine exceeding great reward.

entries.title: Mark 10:32
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As most willing of his way, though he went now to suffer. Shew we like forwardnesse, and say, I am in prison till I am in prison. (Act. & Mon.)

entries.title: Mark 10:35
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: One said he could have what he would of God: And why? but because he would ask nothing, but what was agreeable to the will of God. Fiat voluntas mea, said Luther in a certain prayer; but then falls off sweetly, Mea voluntas, Domine, quia tua. One saith of Luther, Vir iste potuit quod voluit apud Deum: That man can doe what (Melch. Adam.) he will with God.

entries.title: Mark 10:39
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
But not of that bitter cup of his Fathers wrath, which he drank off in his passion. Only the Saints fill up that which is behind of the sufferings of Christ, Colos. 1. 24. [ilegible] [ilegible] [ilegible].

Yee shall be baptized] And come out of the waters of affliction with as little hurt as a babe doth out of the water in baptisme, by the help of divine grace.

entries.title: Mark 10:42
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: All earthly ruledomes are but shewes and shadowes, to that of God. Qui videntur (Oi [ilegible].) imperare: They doe but seem to rule.

entries.title: Mark 10:46
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Named and celebrated in the Gospel, when many mighty Monarchs are utterly forgotten, or else lie shrouded in the sheet of shame.

entries.title: Mark 10:48
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: True faith works its way through many obstacles, as the clouded sun doth.

entries.title: Mark 10:50
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Though a beggar, he stood not upon the losse of his coat; but for joy of his calling [ilegible] it from him. So Joh. 4. 28. Heb. 12. 1.

entries.title: Mark 11:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: AS if it had been done on set purpose. Here was a wheel within a wheel, Ezek. 1. the better to convince the stubborn Jewes of his Kingly office.

entries.title: Mark 11:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: See here six severall arguments of our Saviours Deity: 1. That he knew there was such an asse-colt. 2. That he sent for it. 3. Fore-saw that (Piscator.) the masters of the colt would question them that fet it. 4. That he professeth himself the Lord of all. 5. That he could tell they would send the colt. 6. That accordingly they did so.

entries.title: Mark 11:12
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This, and that he knew not but that there were figs on the tree, declare him to be true Man.

entries.title: Mark 11:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: viz. Of ripe figs; but if he could have found but green figs only, he would at that time have been glad of them. Hee looked for somewhat from that great shew of leaves. But the old Proverb became true, Great bruit, little fruit.

entries.title: Mark 11:17
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: He inveighs against the same fault with the same arguments, as before, Joh. 2.

entries.title: Mark 11:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: So the fig-tree bare farre better fruit now that it was dryed, then when it was green and flourishing. [ilegible] nos Patres, tum docentes, tum labentes: (Aug.) The Saints teach us, as by their instructions, so by their infirmities.

entries.title: Mark 11:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Severall gestures in prayer are described, not prescribed in Gods Book. The word here rendred stand, importeth a presenting ones self before the ([ilegible].) Lord, whether he stand, sit, or kneel, &c.

entries.title: Mark 11:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: So when the enemies of Reformation demand what we mean by so doing, ask them what they think of that we doe? Is it from heaven, or of men? If from heaven, why doe not they approve it? If of men, why doe not they disprove it by the Scriptures? Bucer and Melancthon framed a form of Reformation according to the truth of the Gospel, with the approbation of the Peers and States of Cullen; (Melch. Adam. in vit. [ilegible].) but the Clergy, though not able to contradict it by good reason, yet rejected it with slander, and said that they had rather chuse to live under the Turkish Government, then under a Magistrate that embraced that Reformation.

entries.title: Mark 12:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: SEe the Notes on Matth. 21. 33.

entries.title: Mark 12:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Properly, they hilded him; but by ([ilegible] [ilegible] excorio, [ilegible]. Gerhard.) a Metonymie, they beat him. Sie [ilegible] vulpem, [ilegible] pellis [ilegible] AEtrahatur: So men beat a Fox, that they may the better hilde him.

entries.title: Mark 12:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Caput. [ilegible], they ([ilegible] Theophylact.) brake his head. Theophylact interpreteth it, They completed their villany, and spent all their spite upon him.

entries.title: Mark 12:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: They will surely be [ilegible] to look him in the [ilegible]. This is the proper signification of ([ilegible]) the word. But sin had [ilegible] an impudency in their faces, that they could blush no more then a Sack-but.

entries.title: Mark 12:13
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As Hunters catch the ([ilegible].) beast in a toyl; as Fowlers catch the bird in a snare, as Saint Matthewes ([ilegible].) word here signifies. Fistula [ilegible], [ilegible] dum decipit auceps.

entries.title: Mark 12:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This tribute the Jewes then paid to the Romanes, as now they doe to the Turks, for the very heads they wear. And yet they had the face to say to our Saviour, Joh. 8. 33. We never were in bondage to any man. But perhaps these Jewes were of the Sect of Judas Gaulonites, who would not be (Ioseph. lib 18. cap. 2.) drawn by any torments to acknowledge any Lord upon earth; beleeving that God only was to be held their Lord and King.

entries.title: Mark 12:24
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And yet they alledged and argued out of Scripture, but upon a false ground; viz. that the state of men should continue in the other world such as it is here, as to eat, drink, marry, generate, &c.

entries.title: Mark 12:26
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Therefore thy God also, if thou walk in the foot-steps of faithfull Abraham, Rom. 4. 23, 24.

entries.title: Mark 12:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: All Christs Disciples must be [ilegible], Questionists, and doe the same to learn, that this Scribe here doth, for a worse purpose.

entries.title: Mark 12:29
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This the wiser Heathens, as Pythagoras, ([ilegible], &c. Pythag.) Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle with his Ens Entium miserere mei (if that were his) acknowledged. Exod. 34. 14. Thou shalt worship [ilegible] other god. Where the word Acher rendred Other, hath R greater then ordinary, to shew the greatnesse of the (Buxtorf. Tiber.) sinne of serving others gods, and to set forth a difference between Acher Other, and Echad One God; One in Three, and Three in One.

entries.title: Mark 12:34
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That he was better then the ([ilegible]. Ennius.) Pharisees used to be. He was Egregiè cordatus homo, and began to lift up his head out of the mud toward heaven.

entries.title: Mark 12:35
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: They were great Genealogists; how was it then that they were no better versed in the Genealogie of Christ? that they could give no better an account of his two-fold nature? Of other things one may be ignorant, and yet be saved: Not so here.

entries.title: Mark 12:36
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The Psalmes then are a part of holy Writ by Christs own testimony, who also Luk. 24. 44. divideth the Old Testament into the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalmes. Yea, Psalmorum liber [ilegible] utilia sunt ex omnibus continet, saith Augustine after Basil: The Psalmes are a treasury of all holy truths.

entries.title: Mark 12:38
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Down to the heels, as Senators, or Counsellors. A garment that Christ himself ware, as ([ilegible]. [ilegible].) being a Citizen or free Denison of Capernaum. But he loved not to go in it, as these Pharisees, these glorious Masters of the Jewes; he affected not this habit more then another out of pride and vainglory, to be looked at, and admired by the vulgar. This they thought a goodly businesse.

entries.title: Mark 12:41
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
He still sits and seeth the condition, gift, and mind of every almes-giver: And weighs all, not by the worth of the gift, but by the will of the Giver. Lycurgus enjoyned the Lacedaemonians to offer small sacrifices. For God, said He, respecteth more the internall devotion, then the externall oblation.

How the people cast mony] Gr. Brasse: the worst was thought ([ilegible]) good enough for God, and his poor. Something men will do, but as little as they can.

entries.title: Mark 12:42
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: A mite is valued of our mony to be three (Godw. Antiq.) parts of one c.

entries.title: Mark 12:43
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
