entries.content: Women are noted in the Parable of the lost Groat to be fond of mony: Widowes especially, and poore Widowes, make much of that little they have, as their ([ilegible].) life, so it is called here, verse 44. even all her life, that is, her livelyhood. All this she cast in, it being rather to and for the service of God, then to the poore. She resolves, as a Widow indeed, to trust wholly in God.

entries.title: Mark 13:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: HUge stones, and so cunningly cimented, and as it were inoculated (Quasi tota [ilegible] ex [ilegible] lapide [ilegible] tantam magnitud. [ilegible]) the one into the other, that a man would have thought and sworn almost, that they had been all but one entire stone. Josephus writeth of these stones, that they were fifteen cubits long, twelve high, and eight broad.

entries.title: Mark 13:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: There's no trusting therefore to Forts and strong-holds, no though they be munitions of rocks; as Esay speaketh; The Jebusites, that jeared David and his forces, were thrown out of their Sion. Babylon, that bore her selfe bold upon her twenty yeers provision laid in for a siege, and upon her high Towers and thick walls, was surprised by Cyrus. So was this goodly Temple by [ilegible], who left onely three towers of this stately edifice unrazed, to declare unto posterity the strength of the place, and valour of the vanquisher. But, sixty five years after, AElius [ilegible] inflicting on the rebelling Jewes a wonderfull flaughter, subverted those remainders, and sprinkled salt upon the foundation.

entries.title: Mark 13:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Or, have an end, that is, be destroyed, ([ilegible].) as vers. 2. Which yet these Apostles held not destroyable till the worlds destruction, as appears [ilegible]. 24.

entries.title: Mark 13:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Not directly to their question, but far better to their edification. This was [ilegible] with our Saviour.

entries.title: Mark 13:7
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Neither of the world, nor of the Temple.

entries.title: Mark 13:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The sorrowes and ([ilegible].) throwes of child-birth; which are nothing so bad at first, as in the birth.

entries.title: Mark 13:10
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: i. e. Among other nations then the Jewes.

entries.title: Mark 13:11
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Conne not your answers as boyes use to doe their Orations and School-exercises, which the Greeks call [ilegible]: whereunto Beza thinks our Saviour here [ilegible].

entries.title: Mark 13:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
The Romane forces, therefore most abominable to God and his Angels, because they desolated the pleasant land, and abolished the true worship of God. See Revel. 17. 4, 5.

Where it ought not] viz. In respect of the Romanes, who did it onely out of ambition and covetousnesse. See Esay 10. 7.

entries.title: Mark 13:19
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Gr. Those dayes shall be affliction: as if the very time were nothing else but [ilegible] it self. See the Notes on Mat. 24. 21.

entries.title: Mark 13:20
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: [ilegible], [ilegible]. ([ilegible].) Not in respect of the divine decree, but 1. of the long miseries that the people had deserved: 2. of the enemies rage, that would have exceeded. See [ilegible]. 1. 13.

entries.title: Mark 13:28
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: We should not rest content with a naturall [ilegible] of the creatures, as bruits doe, but pick some spirituall matter out of every sensible object. Thus [ilegible] Master [ilegible] when the Sun shined on his face now lying on his death bed, fell into a sweet meditation of the glory (D. Hall's Art of Divine Meditation.) of God, and his approaching joy.

entries.title: Mark 13:30
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Begun they were in the destruction of Jerusalem, carried on by the enemies rage against the Church, and to be ended with the last age of the Church, which begins at the coming of Christ in the flesh.

entries.title: Mark 13:34
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: That the rest did their work.

entries.title: Mark 13:35
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: But come he will to judgement, as sure as that hee hath destroyed Jerusalem: This is a pledge of the other.

entries.title: Mark 13:37
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: What Serbidius Scevola was wont to say of the Civill Law, holds more true of the divine Law: Jus civile scriptum est vigilantibus, non dormitantibus: The Law was written for those that observe to obey it.

entries.title: Mark 14:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: TWo dayes after the former discourse. This Sun of righteousnesse shone most amiably toward his going down.

entries.title: Mark 14:2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: And yet they did it on the feast-day, as loth to lose the opportunity then offered them by Judas the traytor: But God had a speciall hand in it, that by the circumstance of time Christ might appeare to be the true Passeover. He was crucified on the very true day of that Feast.

entries.title: Mark 14:3
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Or pure, right, sincere, ([ilegible] Meliùs, [ilegible]. [ilegible]. ex Hartungi Criticis.) not sophisticate, or adulterate; so Theophylact interprets it. But [ilegible] saith it was spikenard of Opis, a Town not farre from Babylon, whence the most precious odours and oyntments were [ilegible] into other parts.

entries.title: Mark 14:5
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
That is, fifty-two French pounds and more, as Budaeus computes it. Shee spared for no cost.

They murmured against her] But Judas began: So dangerous ([ilegible] Murmur & fremitus indignantium [ilegible]. Beza.) a thing it is to converse with hypocrites. One rotten sheep may [ilegible] the rest: Uvaque conspectâ livorem ducit ab una. Great danger there is if not of infection, yet of defection. Peter, by his halting, compelled others to doe so too, Gal. 2.

entries.title: Mark 14:14
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: In a private house; for the whole City was then turned into a great Inne, for the receipt of strangers that came up to the Feast.

entries.title: Mark 14:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: For his own particular: for otherwise in respect of the glory of Gods justice, in that mans righteous condemnation, good it was that he was born.

entries.title: Mark 14:25
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: [ilegible] I will not, not, not [ilegible], So Heb. 13. 5. I will not, not, not forsake thoe. Our Saviour here seemeth to allude to that grace-cup (as they call it) after which they might not eat any thing more, till the day following.

entries.title: Mark 14:31
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: The Syriack addeth Mari, that is, Domine mi. And this he affirmed magis ex abundanti. So did Pendleton the Apostate, when hee said to Sanders the Martyr with (Act. & Mon. 1363.) greatest vehemency, I will see the [ilegible] drop of this grease of mine molten away, and the last gobbet of this flesh consumed to ashes, before. I will forsake God and his truth.

entries.title: Mark 14:36
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Father, Father, with greatest earnestnesse. This was an effectuall prayer, had he said no more. God can feel breath in prayer, Lam. 3. 56.

Not that I will, but, &c.] [ilegible] emphatica, saith Beza

entries.title: Mark 14:37
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: How then wilt thou die with me? So how will they endure wounds for Christ, that cannot endure words? See Jer. 12. 5.

entries.title: Mark 14:40
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: They were ashamed to excuse it, yet fell again into it.

entries.title: Mark 14:41
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: If you can at least, or have any mind to it, with so many swords and halberds about your eares. They were in heavinesse, and yet are sharply reproved for relapsing so oft into the same sinne. Let not us be more mild then Christ was; but deal freely and faithfully with all.

entries.title: Mark 14:47
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Beza gathereth from this Text, that Mark received not this Gospel from Peter; because Peter would no lesse have confessed this rashnesse in himselfe, then hee had done his denyall of his Master.

And cut off his eare] This was his indiscreet zeal, proceeding (Piscat.) [ilegible] affectu carnis, non ab afflatu Spiritus sancti: From the flesh, not Spirit.

entries.title: Mark 14:61
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: So God is called, because to be everlastingly blessed and praised of Men and Angels. Hence God is frequently set forth in the Commentaries of the Hebrew Doctors by [ilegible], He that is blessed. So [ilegible] begins his Canticle with Blessed [ilegible] the Lord God, &c. Luk. 1. 68.

entries.title: Mark 14:63
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: So they used to doe in case of blasphemy, to signifie that their very hearts were rent with grief at so sad a hearing.

entries.title: Mark 14:64
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: As a Blasphemer, because he made himself the Son of God. This may comfortably assure [ilegible] that we are freed by Christ from that crime of blasphemy we stand guilty of, for affecting a Deity in our first Parents.

entries.title: Mark 14:65
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Est hic sarcasmus amarulentissimus. [ilegible]. This is a most bitter [ilegible].

entries.title: Mark 14:68
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Thinking to steale away: and here he heard the Cock, but recanted not.

entries.title: Mark 14:71
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Let him that stands, take heed, &c. [ilegible] autem, si pavebis. God had a sweet providence in all this, that Peter might be an eye-witnesse of our Saviours sufferings.

entries.title: Mark 14:72
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Or, adding to his greif, (Augens, id [ilegible], [ilegible] flevit [ilegible].) proportioning his sorrow to his sin: Or, throwing his garment over his head (which was the garb of deep mourners, 2 Sam. 16. 30. Esth. 6. 12.) so Theophylact expounds it. Or, prorupit in fletum. He [ilegible] out and wept.

entries.title: Mark 15:1
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: THey thought once to have deferred his execution till after the [ilegible], chap. 14. 2. But their malice was wrestlesse: as his was that said, he would not away till he saw the Martyrs (the [ilegible] (Act. [ilegible] Mon. [ilegible]. 1119.) he called him) heart out.

entries.title: Mark 15:6
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Or, at each great Feast: viz. at the ([ilegible].) Passeover, Pentecost, and Tabernacles, The reason of this custome see in Notes on Matt. 27. 15.

entries.title: Mark 15:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Purposely to move the people to Pity him, and therefore brought him forth so misused with, Behold the man. But this was ill done of Pilate neverthelesse: As was also his comparing him with Barabbas, though with [ilegible] so to have delivered him. For we may not do evill, that good may come thereof.

entries.title: Mark 15:21
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
We all come off heavily, ([ilegible] cogunt invitum.) and shrink in the shoulder when called to carry the Crosse, as Peter did, Joh. 21. 18.

The Father of Alexander and Rufus] Men famously known in the Church, and therefore here but named only. God will recompence even involuntary services.

entries.title: Mark 15:23
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This was not the same potion with that verse 36. and Matth. 27. 48. but another.

entries.title: Mark 15:33
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Portending doubtlesse those dreadfull calamities that were coming upon this perverse people: according to Esay 5. 30. & 8. 22. Lam. 3. 1, 2. But clearly shewing Gods heavy displeasure against his Son our Surety, which made him also cry out with a loud voice in the next verse, as [ilegible] so far forsaken, as not afforded the common-benefit of Sunnelight.

entries.title: Mark 15:42
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Their preparation to the Sabbath began at three aclock in the afternoon. The Jewes of [ilegible] (Buxtorf.) began their. Sabbath sooner then others: those at Tsepphore continued it longer; adding de profano ad sacrum. Among our Forefathers at the ringing of the Bell to Prayer on Saturday-evening, the husbandman would give over his labour in the field, and the tradesman his work in the shop, and set themselves to [ilegible] for the Sabbath.

entries.title: Mark 15:43
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: It was boldly done indeed, thus to oppose, not the Jewes only, but Pilate in that which [ilegible] had done to Christ. Good blood will not bely it self.

entries.title: Mark 16:1-2
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: AS God on the first day of the week drew the World out of that abhorred estate of nothing, and brought light out of [ilegible]: so did Christ, on that day, draw his people out of an (2 Tim. 1.) estate worse then nothing, and brought life and immortality to light by the Gospel.

entries.title: Mark 16:4
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: Or, as some read it, when they looked up: for till now they may seem either to have gone plodding on with their eyes downward; or else to have looked on one another, as people use to do when they are conferring.

entries.title: Mark 16:8
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: whom they met with, but hastened to the Disciples.

entries.title: Mark 16:9
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: This honour done to Mary Magdalene, Mark relateth more at large then the rest: 'though otherwise, mostly, he be more brief then the rest.

entries.title: Mark 16:15
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
Eckins hence blasphemously [ilegible], ([ilegible]. [ilegible]. [ilegible]. [ilegible].) that Christ did never command his Apostles to write, but to preach only.

[ilegible] every creature] That is, to Man, who is a little world, an Epitome of every creature. 2. To the Gentiles also, who had been denyed this favour of the Gospel, as if they had been none of Gods creatures.

entries.title: Mark 16:16
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content:
That which you preach.

And is baptized] As content to give up himself to Christ, and to receive his mark, making a publike profession of the faith.

He that beleeveth not] He saith not, or, Is not baptized; for it is not the want, but the contempt of baptisme that damneth. Unbeleef is a bloudy sin, Heb. 10. 26. a heavie sin, Joh. 3. 19. a most ingratefull, inexcusable sinne, such as shuts a man up close prisoner in the dark dungeon of the Law, unto unavoydable destruction, Gal. 3. 23.

entries.title: Mark 16:18
entries.author: John Trapp (1601–1669)
entries.content: No more shall the deadly poyson of sinne hurt those that have drunk it, if they belong to God; provided that they cast it up again quickly by Confession, and meddle no more with such a mischeif.
